parts.title: Pottery course enquiry
parts.contextVi: Một người đàn ông gọi điện đến trung tâm cộng đồng để hỏi và đăng ký khóa học làm gốm.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Good morning, Willowbrook Community Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Hello. I saw a poster for your beginners' pottery course, and I'd like to find out about joining it.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Of course. We still have places on the autumn course. Can I take your details first? What's your surname?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: It's Brenton.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Could you spell that for me, please?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Sure. That's B-R-E-N-T-O-N.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Thank you, Mr Brenton. And a contact number?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My mobile is oh one six one, five five five, oh one four seven.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Lovely. Now, the course runs on three evenings, Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Which would suit you?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Tuesday would be best, because I finish work early that day.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Oh, I'm sorry, the Tuesday class is already full. Wednesday has places, and so does Thursday.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I play football on Wednesdays, so Thursday it is.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Great. The poster says the class starts at seven o'clock, but we've changed it, so it's seven fifteen and finishes at nine thirty.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And how much is the course?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: It used to be seventy-five pounds, but the price went up this term, so it's eighty-five pounds for ten weeks, including all the clay.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's fine. Do I need to bring anything?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Just an apron, as clay gets everywhere. All the tools are provided, and you don't need a towel because there are sinks in the studio.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Where exactly is the centre?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: We're on Mill Lane, just past the post office.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And is there somewhere to park?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: The small car park at the front is for staff, and the street opposite the café is always busy. Most people use the car park behind the library, which is only a two-minute walk.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Good. And which room is the class in?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Studio twelve, on the first floor. Studio two on the ground floor is for the painting class, so please don't go there by mistake.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: One more thing. Are there any discounts?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Yes, pensioners get ten percent off, but unfortunately students don't. I'll send you a confirmation by email. Thanks for calling, Mr Brenton.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

questions.explain: Daniel đánh vần: 'That's B-R-E-N-T-O-N' → Brenton.

parts.title: Welcome to Kestrel Valley Nature Park
parts.contextVi: Một nhân viên công viên giới thiệu cho du khách về lịch sử, giờ mở cửa, bản đồ và sự kiện của công viên thiên nhiên.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Good morning everyone, and welcome to Kestrel Valley Nature Park. Before you set off, I'll give you a quick introduction. The park is only twenty-five years old, but the land has a long history. Many people assume it was farmland, and some of the stone walls do come from old farms, but most of the lake was actually created when a quarry was flooded after the stone workers left in the nineteen seventies.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Opening times are worth knowing. The car park opens at eight, for walkers and dog owners, but the visitor centre, where you can pick up maps, doesn't open until nine. The café opens even later, at ten, so you might want to bring a snack if you arrive early.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Entry to the park is free, and so is parking, which surprises many visitors. The only thing you pay for is our guided walks, which are six pounds per person and last about ninety minutes. Bird-watching and walking on the main paths cost nothing at all.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Now let me take you round the map. The first aid point is right next to the main gate, so you'll pass it as you come in. The café used to be in the visitor centre, but it moved last year, and it's now inside the old barn, the stone building you can see in the middle of the map.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: The toilets are behind the visitor centre, not in it, which confuses a lot of people, so look for the small wooden building. If you're keen on birds, many visitors expect the hide to be along the river path, but the best one is actually beside the lake, so head there early in the morning.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: If you'd like to explore on two wheels, bike hire is run by a separate company, and you'll find it at the south entrance, which is the opposite end of the park from the main gate. It's about a twenty-minute walk from here, so you may prefer to drive round.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: A few requests before you go. Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a lead because of the nesting birds, and you're welcome to take photographs of the wild flowers. What we really ask is that you don't feed the ducks. Many people like to throw bread, but it makes them ill, so please don't.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Finally, some events next month. We were going to run an astronomy night, but it's been cancelled because of the weather forecast. Instead we have a bat walk on the twelfth, and a photography workshop on the nineteenth. Pond-dipping is only in summer, and the craft market doesn't happen until December. Enjoy your visit.

parts.title: Supermarket packaging presentation
parts.contextVi: Hai sinh viên trao đổi với giảng viên về bài thuyết trình nhóm về bao bì nhựa trong siêu thị.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Hello both, thanks for coming. You wanted to talk about your presentation on supermarket packaging. How's it going?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Quite well, although we nearly chose a different topic. At first I suggested food waste, but Priya pointed out that almost every group in previous years has done it, so we went for plastic packaging instead.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: It also gives us a local angle. We're comparing three supermarkets in the town centre.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Good. And how are you collecting your data? Last time you mentioned interviewing shoppers.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That was the plan, but the store managers refused permission to stand outside their shops. So we've put a questionnaire online and we're sharing it through the university's social media.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: That's reasonable, but be careful. An online survey may attract mostly students, so your results might not represent ordinary shoppers. You need to mention that limitation in your talk.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We did think of that. We're aiming for about two hundred responses, and we'll ask our families to share the link with their neighbours and friends as well.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Good idea. Now, let's look at your sources. What have you found so far?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: The council report looked ideal at first, because it has figures for every supermarket in the region.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: True, but it was published in twenty fourteen, so most of the packaging policies it describes have since changed.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Then there's the Greenfield Stores brochure about reducing plastic. It's full of impressive claims, but of course it only tells the company's side of the story.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Yes, treat that with caution. What about academic sources?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: There's a journal article on recycling rates. It's very thorough, but frankly the statistics are so complicated that we had to ask a lecturer to explain them to us.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: And we found a newspaper article saying supermarkets waste thousands of tonnes of plastic, but it gives no evidence for that figure, so we can't really use it.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: That's sensible. Now, the structure of the presentation. How long do you have?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Fifteen minutes for the talk itself, then five minutes for questions, so twenty in total.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Fine. For your conclusion, I'd suggest two things. First, a clear recommendation for the supermarkets, and second, an honest discussion of the weaknesses of your own research. You don't need to repeat all your survey results, and photographs belong earlier in the talk.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That makes sense. When should we send you a draft of the slides?

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: By next Friday, please. I'm at a conference on Thursday, so email it and I'll comment over the weekend. And do rehearse before the real thing, ideally in front of other students.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We'll do that. I'll book a seminar room for Monday afternoon.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Thank you, Dr Alvarez. This has been really helpful.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: You're welcome. Good luck with the survey.

parts.title: Green roofs
parts.contextVi: Một bài giảng đại học về lịch sử, các loại hình, lợi ích và hạn chế của mái nhà xanh.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Today I'd like to talk about green roofs, that is, roofs deliberately covered with vegetation. Although they seem like a modern idea, the earliest examples are the turf roofs of traditional Scandinavian houses, where a layer of soil provided insulation against the cold. They were largely forgotten during the nineteenth century, until German engineers revived the concept in the nineteen sixties.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Modern green roofs come in two main types. Extensive roofs have only a thin layer of growing material, usually under fifteen centimetres, and are planted mainly with a hardy plant called sedum. They are light and cheap. Intensive roofs, by contrast, can support shrubs and even small trees, but they require much stronger structures underneath, as well as regular irrigation.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Let me now turn to the benefits, and the first is stormwater management. In a heavy rainstorm, a green roof can absorb up to eighty percent of the water that falls on it, which relieves the pressure on city drains and so reduces the risk of flooding. This is why a number of European cities have encouraged them.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: The second benefit relates to temperature. Cities are warmer than the surrounding countryside, an effect known as the urban heat island. Plants cool the air through evaporation, and measurements in one Australian city showed that green roof surfaces were up to thirty degrees cooler than conventional ones on a summer afternoon.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Third, there is biodiversity. Even small roofs attract insects, and so-called brownfield roofs, which imitate abandoned industrial land, have attracted rare beetles, as well as nesting birds. In some cities, these roofs now act as stepping stones between parks that would otherwise be isolated.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: However, there are drawbacks. The most obvious is cost, since installation can be three times that of a conventional roof. There is also the matter of maintenance, because weeds can damage the waterproof membrane. Some owners worry about leaks, but research suggests that properly installed roofs actually last longer, since the vegetation protects the roof from ultraviolet light.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Despite these concerns, several countries have made green roofs compulsory in certain cases. The best-known example is the Swiss city of Basel, where the regulations require all new flat roofs to be green. As a result, the city now has one of the highest proportions of green roofs in Europe.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: To sum up, green roofs are an old idea that has been given new life by modern technology. Their value lies not in any single advantage but in the combination of water control, cooling and wildlife habitat. In the next session, we'll look at how their performance can be measured in practice.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Good morning, Harbourview Climbing Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Hello. I'm thinking of joining the centre, and I wondered if you could tell me how it all works.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Of course. Can I take your name first, so I can set up an enquiry record?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Yes, it's Daniel Brennick.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Could you spell the surname for me, please?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Sure. That's B-R-E-N-N-I-C-K.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Thank you. And if you're wondering where we are, we're at fourteen Calder Road, just behind the old bus station. Please don't confuse it with Calder Street, which is on the other side of town.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Thanks, I'll make a note of that. Is there anything I have to do before I can start climbing?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Yes, every new member has to complete a safety induction. We have places on Wednesday evening, if that suits you.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Wednesday is difficult for me, because I work late. Is Thursday possible?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Yes, Thursday is fine. The first session at five thirty is already full, so I'd book you into the later one, at six thirty in the evening. It takes about ninety minutes.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's perfect. Is there anything I should bring?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Just comfortable sports clothes. We lend out climbing shoes for free during the induction. But do bring a padlock for your locker, because we provide the lockers but not the locks.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: OK, a padlock. I'll buy one on the way.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Now I'll ask a few questions for the form. How did you hear about us?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My sister told me about you. She joined last year. I did see your advert on a bus too, but she's the reason I called.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Lovely. And what kind of climbing interests you most? We have bouldering, rope climbing and a fitness area.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I'd like to try rope climbing eventually, but I've never done it. I'll start with bouldering, since I don't need a partner for that.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: That's sensible. Now, for membership, the standard one is fifty-two pounds a month and lets you come at any time. Off-peak is thirty-eight pounds, but only on weekdays before four o'clock. And there's a weekend-only one at thirty pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I finish work at half past five, and I'm busy on Saturdays, so off-peak and weekend-only are no good for me. I'll take the standard one.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Great. The joining fee is normally twenty pounds, but this month we're offering it at fifteen pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Excellent. Thank you very much, Megan. I'll see you on Thursday.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Goodbye, Daniel. See you then.

parts.title: A new park opens in the city
parts.contextVi: Một người dẫn chương trình radio địa phương giới thiệu công viên mới sắp mở cửa trong thành phố.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Welcome to the community slot on Greenline Radio. This week, the long-awaited Marlow Fields Park finally opens to the public on Saturday the twelfth of April. You may have seen the eleventh of April on some websites, but that's only a private preview for local councillors, so please don't turn up on Friday.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Many people believe the city council paid for the whole project, but in fact most of the money, about seventy percent, came from a national lottery grant. The council paid for the playground, and a few local businesses donated the trees.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: The site has an interesting past. It was a tram depot for many years, and later a car factory, which closed in the nineteen nineties. For the last ten years or so, before building began, the land was used as a temporary car park, which is why the ground needed so much work.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Now let me take you on a tour. When you come in through the East Gate, the first thing you'll see is a children's maze made of tall hedges. It's already popular with the families who've seen it growing. Further on, at the Lakeside, there's a wooden bird hide, where you can watch ducks and herons without disturbing them.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Walk on to Orchard Corner, where old apple and pear trees have been kept, and you'll find several picnic shelters, so a shower won't spoil your lunch. If you're feeling energetic, climb up to the Hilltop, where artists have placed eight sculptures along a winding path, and the view over the city is wonderful.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: The last area is Old Station Square, by the West Gate, where a small café will serve hot drinks and cakes. An outdoor gym was planned for that area, but the council decided it was too expensive, and the bike repair stand has been postponed until next year.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Opening hours: from April to September, the park is open from six in the morning until nine at night. In winter, the closing time was going to be five o'clock, but after requests from residents who walk home from work, the gates will now close at six.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: And finally, the opening weekend. On Saturday there'll be a guided history walk, and on Sunday morning children can join a tree planting session. We had hoped for live music too, but unfortunately the band has pulled out. Free bike checks won't start until May. See you there!

parts.title: Planning a presentation on food waste
parts.contextVi: Hai sinh viên thảo luận với giảng viên về bài thuyết trình cho môn học về phát triển bền vững.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation for the sustainability module. Last week you were planning to look at plastic packaging, I think?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We were, but when we did a literature search, we found loads of recent studies already. We didn't think we could add anything new.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Our first worry was that the topic was too broad, but the real problem was how much had been published. So we've switched to food waste.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: That sounds sensible. What kind of data do you have in mind?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: I thought we could ask supermarket managers, to get figures on how much they throw away.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Realistically, I doubt they'd agree, and you only have three weeks. But the campus café has weighed its waste every day for two years, and the manager is happy to share the records.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That's much easier. Though I'd still like to look at households as well, because honestly I think families throw away far more food than shops do, and that's where the real problem is.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Maybe, but the café figures give us numbers we can trust. Household waste is mostly guesswork.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: You could add a short survey for the household side. Now, the format. The slot is twenty minutes altogether, but that includes five minutes of questions, so you have fifteen minutes to present.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Fifteen, OK. For the slides, I think photographs of bins full of food would have more impact than graphs. People remember pictures.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Some, certainly, but I'd keep graphs for the main comparisons. And keep your introduction brief, no more than two minutes. Audiences lose patience if you take too long to reach your findings.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We should rehearse with a timer, then. Last time we ran over by six minutes and lost marks.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Good idea. I read the draft outline you sent. The structure is clear, but the conclusion is weak. You describe the problem well, yet you don't suggest what the café could do differently.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: We can add some recommendations. We also ran a pilot survey last week, with fifty students.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: How did it go?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Mostly fine, but nearly everyone who answered was under twenty-five, so we've hardly got any older people. And some questions confused people. Nobody understood what we meant by 'avoidable waste'.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Those are both fixable. I wouldn't worry about the length, ten questions is fine, and there's no need to translate it, since you're surveying English-speaking course members.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: So what should we do before the next tutorial?

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Email me the revised outline by Friday if you can, but first of all go and meet the café manager, and ask which weeks' figures are the most reliable.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We'll do that tomorrow. Thanks, Dr Marsh.

options: They could not find any data.

parts.title: The history of glass
parts.contextVi: Một bài giảng đại học về lịch sử của thủy tinh, từ thủy tinh tự nhiên đến quy trình sản xuất hiện đại.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about glass, a material so familiar that we rarely think about where it came from. Let's begin with natural glass. When volcanic lava cools very quickly, it can solidify before crystals have time to form, and the best known example of this is obsidian. Early peoples all over the world used it to make sharp blades and, above all, arrowheads.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: When was glass first made deliberately? Some older books say Egypt, and Egyptian glassmakers were certainly skilled, but the earliest evidence we have points to Mesopotamia, the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Those early craftsmen could not blow glass. Instead they shaped small containers by wrapping soft glass around a core of clay, which was scraped out afterwards.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: The real revolution came in the Roman period, with the invention of glassblowing in the first century before Christ. Blowing air through a tube allowed craftsmen to produce vessels far more quickly, and as a result glass became much cheaper, so that ordinary families, not only the wealthy, could afford cups and bottles.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: The Romans also produced the first window glass, but it was thick and cloudy. Interestingly, the earliest windows were not installed in homes at all, but in bathhouses, where they helped to keep the heat in while still letting some light through.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: Let's jump forward to the Middle Ages, when Venice became the glass capital of Europe. In the thirteenth century, the city ordered its glassmakers to move to the island of Murano. The official reason was the danger of fire, since furnaces burned day and night in a city of wooden buildings, although many historians suspect the rulers also wanted to protect their trade secrets.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: In the seventeenth century, the English maker George Ravenscroft transformed the industry. By adding lead oxide to the mixture, he produced a heavy, brilliant glass which we still call lead crystal. It was softer to cut and decorate, and it quickly became fashionable across Europe.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: The next major change came in the nineteen fifties, when Alastair Pilkington developed the float process. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin, and because tin is so dense and perfectly level, the glass spreads out into a flat, smooth sheet. Before this, large sheets had to be ground and polished by hand, which was slow and wasteful.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: Finally, a word about sustainability. Glass is made from sand, soda ash and limestone, all of them abundant, and unlike many materials it can be recycled endlessly without any loss of quality. Yet in many countries only a fraction of bottles is collected. Next week, we'll turn to metals and ask a similar question.
